City Hotel', and Andreas has him buying the Tremont House block from General Beaubien and building the five houses known as Egan's Row, which is why a physician is also one of the town's builders. The register enters him six times between 3 September 1835 and 1 January 1836 for 720 acres at $900, which is that dealer at work. He is the ONLY Egan the register holds and the only adult Egan of the surname the layer holds. Upheld.

Upheld on the second-document arm, with the register's own family shape agreeing. The town holds John Foot on two contemporary civic rolls that BRACKET the entry — the tax list of 1833, the same year as the two school-section rows of 22 October 1833, and the poll of 1835 after it — and Fergus 1839 prints 'Foot, John I[.], blacksmith, Randolph street, near State', which supplies a trade and a street the register never had. What makes the pair worth more than two bare names is the ANDREWS WILLIAM test: the register sells to a FOOT JOHN and, separately, to a FOOT STAN, and the layer holds a John Foot and an S. Foot — the two records agree on the shape of the surname, and cohort A upheld FOOT STAN as Starr Foot on the same page of reasoning. A blacksmith taking two town lots at the school-section sale for $190 is consistent with everything the town holds of him.

The town elected this man to office ten months after the entry, and the entry is ground inside the town. The Chicago Democrat of 13 August 1834 reports that 'Messrs. John H. Kinzie, G[ordon S. Hub]bard, J. K. Boyer, Ebenezer G[oodrich and J.] S. C. Hogan, were elected Trustees of this Town, for the term of one year' — a named Chicago TOWN TRUSTEE, not a name in a list — and the poll of 1834 holds him independently. The register's single row is lot 1 of block 93 of the school section, bought at the town's own sale of 22 October 1833 for $100: a trustee-to-be buying a town lot at the town's sale. The forename is uncommon and printed in full on both sides, and the layer holds exactly one Ebenezer Goodrich where the register holds three Goodriches it discriminates by forename. Cohort A refused GOODRICH CHAUNCEY, which is a different question: there the town held no Chauncey at all and an initial chose.

The full spelling of a purchaser cohort A already upheld abbreviated, and the PEARSONS reasoning applies unchanged: upholding HADDOCK E H and refusing HADDOCK EDWARD H would be incoherent, since the abbreviated spelling was upheld precisely because the town prints the forename whole. The MIDDLE INITIAL H is on both sides and Fergus 1839 prints it out — 'Haddock, Edward H., commission merchant, South Water st'. The town holds him five times besides: the tax list of 1833, the poll of 1834 ('Haddock, Edward E.', the same man's forename whole), the poll of 1835, three printings in the Democrat of 1834, and the 1840 census. The tax list of 1833 and the poll of 1835 bracket both rows, 25 October 1833 and 27 June 1835. A commission merchant taking eighty acres at the ring is consistent with the trade the card holds.

The town's whole record of George Hall is that somebody else repudiated a note owed to him. The Chicago Democrat of 29 July 1835 prints a caution 'against purchasing a Note, given by me to George Hall, dated June 24. 1835, for fifty dollars' — and the advertiser's own name is sheared off at the crop edge, so even the other party to it is not named. That is ONE reading, it is the ONLY thing in the corpus that names him, there is no directory line in any of the three volumes, no civic roll, no census, no trade and no street. The card's own present_on_scene_date reads `uncertain` for exactly this reason: the earliest source that names him is later than 1 July 1835. Two register rows of 27 June 1835, 160 acres, Residence UNKNOWN, against one press mention: a bare name on each side, which the rule refuses however close the dates fall. Refused, and the 160 acres come back off the card.

The MIDDLE INITIAL is on both sides, the town prints the middle name in full, and the man was the county's own recorder. The register holds exactly one Hamilton, spelled RICHARD J; the town holds Richard Jones Hamilton on the poll of 1833 ('Hamilton, R. J.'), the tax list of 1833 and the poll of 1834 ('Hamilton, Richard J.'), all three of them contemporary with the two school-section rows of 22 and 25 October 1833, and the printed record carries him forward without a break — three Democrat notices of 1834 ('Hon.', 'Col.'), Fergus 1839 'Hamilton, Rich'd J., clerk circuit court, Clark st cor. Randolph', Fergus 1843 'Hamilton, Richard Jones', Norris 1844, the 1840 census. He was clerk and recorder of Cook County from its organisation in 1831, which is to say the officer through whose hands land records passed. Upheld on the middle initial and the bracket together.

The KIMBALL WALTER shape: the man signs his own name, with the initial the register writes, in the town's own paper. The Chicago Democrat of 18 March 1834 carries a signed dissolution notice — 'The Co-partnership of Taylor & Handy was this day dissolved by mutual consent … H. S. HANDY, CHARLES TAYLOR. Chicago, Feb. 1, 1834' — which is a Chicago firm, a partner and a dated Chicago address over his signature, sixteen months before the register enters HANDY HENRY S for 240 acres on 27 June and 10 September 1835. Fergus's old-settler death notices hold him after, as 'Handy, Maj. Henry S.', printing the same middle initial a third time. Two independent town-side documents and the middle initial on both sides. It is the weakest uphold in the cohort and is marked so: there is no directory line, no civic roll and no Residence column, and the ruling rests on the signature and the death notice alone.

MIDDLE INITIAL on both sides, and the register's two spellings of this man mirror the town's own two habits. The town prints 'Harmon, C. L.' on the poll of 1834 and 'Chas. L. Harmon' on the 1837 election return; Fergus 1843 prints both a business card, 'C L. HARMON, commission merchant and wholesale grocer', and the roll entry 'Harmon, Charles Loomis, dry goods and groceries, 145 South Water'; Norris 1844's advertiser pages print 'C. L. Harmon'. The poll of 1834 falls between the two register rows. A wholesale grocer and dry-goods merchant taking a town lot at the school-section sale of 22 October 1833 for $130 is the trade the card already asserts doing what the card says it did. The register holds five Harmon spellings and the layer three Harmons, and the L is what separates this one from both Deweys.

Ruled with HARMON CHARLES L and it goes the same way, which is not the default — cohort C1's BROWN WM is what happens when a barer spelling is allowed to ride on a fuller one. It does not apply here because THIS SPELLING IS NOT BARER: CHAS L carries the middle initial, and the contraction 'Chas.' is precisely the form the 1837 election return and Norris 1844's advertiser card print for this man. The single row of 8 August 1835, 80.45 acres for $100.55, is upheld on the same middle initial and the same trade as the fuller spelling. Cohort A's abbreviated-and-full habit (HADDOCK E H / HADDOCK EDWARD H) is doing real work here rather than being assumed: the two spellings agree on the token that discriminates.

The MIDDLE INITIAL on both sides with the middle name printed in full behind it, and the Residence column reading COOK with a town-side partner to check it against. Fergus 1839 prints 'Harmon, Dr. Elijah D.' and Fergus 1843 'Harmon, Elijah Dewey, physician, bds C. L. Harmon [died January 3, 1869, aged 80]' — the whole middle name, the trade the card holds, and an age that puts birth about 1788, which agrees with Andreas's Bennington, Vermont, 20 August 1782 to within a printer's rounding of a death notice. The layer holds no second Elijah Harmon and the register no second Elijah. One of the two rows of 2 October 1834 states COOK, and cohort B's rule for that column — it needs a town-side partner — is met by the directories' printing of the same initial. Andreas has him pre-empting one hundred and forty acres with a northern boundary near Sixteenth Street, which is the same physician buying ground south of the town that the register's SWFR of section 22 is.

Ruled beside HARMON ISAAC D and it goes the OTHER way, which is the point of ruling paired spellings together. This row of 24 October 1833 prints the forename bare, with no middle initial, and the town's own printed record holds TWO Isaac Harmons: Fergus 1839's 'Harmon, Isaac D., dry goods merchant, 8 Clark street' and Fergus 1843's 'Harmon, Isaac Newton, with C. L. Harmon [died Nov. 8, 1891]'. The card's own crosswalk already records the collision — its evidence_against reads 'CONTESTED: 2 residents of 1835 meet this one entry on that rule, and at most one of them is the person printed'. The layer holds one Isaac Harmon because the layer is THIN, not because the town had one, which is BROWN WM exactly. The argument that would have upheld it — that a man 'with C. L. Harmon' in 1843 was likely too young to buy a $163 town lot in 1833 — is not taken, because Fergus prints his death and no age, and an unprinted age is a guess. Refused; the fuller spelling stands.

Cohort A's lesson run backwards and it holds: where the town's card carries only bare forenames, the DIRECTORY supplies the initial, and it is that printing which upholds. The card's own readings are all bare — 'HARMON, ISAAC' on the muster roll of 1832, 'Isaac Harmon' in the Democrat of 17 December 1833, 'Harmon, Isaac' in the Democrat of 5 August 1835 — and Fergus 1839 prints 'Harmon, Isaac D., dry goods merchant, 8 Clark street', which is the only place on the town's side the D appears. The register writes ISAAC D. The two Democrat printings bracket the row of 22 October 1833 on both sides, ten months before and twenty-one months after. A dry-goods merchant taking a town lot at the school-section sale for $130 is consistent with the trade. Upheld on the middle initial; the bare spelling two days later is refused above.

The PEARSONS pattern, and the largest carry in the cohort. The MIDDLE INITIAL K is on both sides and the town prints the name whole twice — Fergus 1839 'Hubbard, Elijah K., BANKER, 47-51 Dearborn st', and Fergus's death notices 'Hubbard, Elijah Kent', died 26 May 1839. The poll of 1835 holds him at Chicago in the same season as the entries, and the Democrat of 5 August 1835 and the American of 1835 print 'E. K. Hubbard' beside them. The twenty-four rows are one hand at work: twenty-three of them fall on 26 and 27 June 1835 and the last on 25 August, 2,428 acres for $3,509.82 — a banker buying at the ring in two afternoons is the trade the card holds doing what the card says it did, not a second Elijah K. Hubbard who happens to share the county and the week. The register's other Hubbards are GURDON S and THOMAS R, both discriminated by initial.

MIDDLE INITIAL on both sides, and no man of 1835 Chicago is held by more documents. The register writes GURDON S; the town prints 'G. S. Hubbard' in the Democrat of 1 April 1834, 'Gordon S. Hubbard' in the same paper of 13 August 1834 electing him a TOWN TRUSTEE, 'Col. G. S. Hubbard' in June 1835, 'Gurdon S. Hubbard' in the American of 4 July 1835, the poll of 1835, the 1840 census head 'Gurdon S. Hubbard', two Fergus 1843 business cards and the roll entry 'Hubbard, Gurdon Saltonstall, forwarding and commission, South Water', and Norris 1844. The single row of 22 October 1833 is 2.90 acres of the school section for $160 — ground inside the town, taken at the town's own sale by a packer and forwarding merchant whose premises were on South Water. The trustee notice of August 1834 is the same column that carries Ebenezer Goodrich, upheld above.

The fuller of a pair cohort A already read as one entry twice — it upheld HUNTER E E and named EDWARD E as the same row read with the Residence column on the fuller reading, so this is the reading that carries the column. MIDDLE INITIAL E on both sides; the town prints the forename whole on the poll of 1834 ('Hunter, Edward E.'), in the Democrat of 6 August 1834 ('Edward E. Hunter') and in Fergus's death notices ('Hunter, Edward E.'), and Fergus 1839 prints a trade and a street, 'Hunter, Edward [E.], deputy-sheriff, ex-justice of peace, Wells st'. One of the three rows of 15 November 1834 states COOK, and cohort B's requirement of a town-side partner for that column is met by the poll of 1834 three months earlier. Upheld.

`letter_list_only` at its plainest, and the directories make it worse rather than better. The card's own note: 'KNOWN ONLY FROM THE POST OFFICE, IN ONE RETURN — the Democrat of 22 October 1834 … a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further.' Cohort C1's warning was to read press_evidence[].list rather than the flag; read here, the flag is right and there is nothing else. Against that, the register prints SAMUEL bare on four rows of September and October 1833, and the printed record holds TWO Samuel Jacksons with middle names the register does not have — Fergus 1839 'Jackson, Samuel T., Government works, near Garrison', Fergus 1843 'Jackson, Samuel Thomas, overseer Chicago harbor' AND 'Jackson, Samuel Ezra, bds Samuel Jackson', both matched to this card as `ambiguous`. The county history's harbour foreman arriving from Buffalo in June 1833 is an enrichment of a name, not a check on a row: it predicts no purchase, and $328 of town lots that autumn is not what it predicts. Refused.

The town gave this man an OFFICE two weeks after the entries and he was advertising in its paper a month after them. Andreas: 'It was during these days that Benjamin Jones was appointed Street Commissioner' — 7 November 1833, the town's first — and the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 carries him as a paying advertiser, which the card calls strong evidence of existence and address in November 1833. The register's four rows are 22 and 24 October 1833, $1,133 of school-section town lots, a fortnight before the appointment. Fergus 1839 prints 'Jones, Benjamin, GROCER, South Water street' and Norris 1844 'Jones, Benjamin, of B. J. & Co.' with the firm's own card: a South Water grocer buying South Water ground at the town's own sale. The forename is printed in full on both sides, the layer holds one Benjamin Jones and the register discriminates its three Joneses by forename. Upheld on the bracket and the trade together.

Upheld on THREE contemporary civic rolls and an uncommon forename printed whole on both sides, and on nothing else — which is stated plainly because the directory evidence here is worthless. The town holds 'Jones, Willard' on the tax list of 1833, the poll of 1834 and the poll of 1835; the tax list is the same year as the two school-section rows of 22 and 25 October 1833 and the polls hold him after, so the rolls bracket the entries on both sides. The layer holds exactly one Willard Jones and the register exactly one JONES WILLARD, where both records hold several plain Williams. The one directory line the crosswalk offers, Fergus 1839's 'Jones, Wm., justice of the peace', is matched `contested` between this man and William Jones and is not used: it cannot corroborate one of two claimants. Upheld on the second-document arm.

The block's BROWN WM, named as such by the ticket before the cohort was read, and the printed record is worse than Brown's. Fergus 1843 prints THREE distinct William Joneses — 'Jones, William [Golden]. (B. J. & Co.)', 'Jones, William Edwin (Ogden & J.)' and 'Jones, William Harrison, clerk, H. W. Bigelow' — and the 1839 line 'Jones, Wm., justice of the peace' is matched `contested` between this man and Willard Jones, who is upheld above. The register's three rows of 24 October 1833 and 5 August 1835 print WILLIAM bare, with no middle initial and UNKNOWN in the Residence column, and the four Democrat printings on the town's side are bare too ('Wm. Jones', 'Jones, Wm.'). The layer holds one William Jones on the commonest surname in the town because the layer is thin. A bare Wm. Jones on a tract row could be any of the three the directory prints or a fourth. Refused; 243.52 acres come back off the card.

The entry is FIVE YEARS EARLIER than the only reading the town holds. ls0019 is 40 acres of canal land bought on 5 October 1830 with UNKNOWN in the Residence column; the card is a G3 projected resident whose whole record is one line of the town's tax list of 1833 — “Kercheval, Benjamin” — and nothing else. There is no trade, no street, no middle initial, no press printing and no directory line: Fergus 1839, Fergus 1843 and Norris 1844 print no Benjamin Kercheval at all, which is the test cohort A found decided all three of its refusals. Nothing on the town's side reaches 1830 or brackets it, so a bare name on a canal-sale row of 1830 meets a bare name on a tax roll of 1833 and the two do not make an identity. The layer's other Kercheval is Gholson, the sub-agent, whose forename the rule correctly refused; that this proposal survived the forename test says only that nobody else of the name is called Benjamin. Refused; the forty acres come back off the card.

The middle initial is printed on BOTH sides and the printed record gives the middle name whole. The register enters KIMBERLY EDMUND S for the E half of the SE of section 32 on 27 June 1835, in the ring; Fergus 1839 prints “Kimberly, Dr. Edmund S., res. N. Water st next Lake House” and Fergus 1843 “Kimberly, Edmund Stoughten, physician, 101 Lake”. The town holds the man many times over and not as a name only: clerk of the incorporation meeting of 5 August 1833, one of the first trustees, the tax list of 1833 and the poll of 1834 (“Kimberly, Dr. E. S.”), a partner in the town's second drug store, and the Democrat of 1 July 1835. The two other Kimberlys the layer holds are Ira and Osa, whose forenames the rule refused, and no second Edmund S. is printed anywhere in this corpus. Upheld on the middle initial and the second document together. THE SISTER SPELLING IS ALREADY ON THIS CARD: the register also prints KIMBERLEY EDMUND S, cohort B upheld it, and T-1001 — closed 10 September 2026 on PR #1079 — merged `kimberley_ed` into this physician, so that ruling now stands against `kimberly_edmund_s` as well. The two spellings are one man on one card and nothing is counted twice.

THE TOWN PRINTS THE FORENAME IN FULL EXACTLY ONCE, and every other reading on the card is an initial that the directory's own pages give to a different man. The card's one contemporary printing is the Democrat of 6 August 1834, “Nehemiah King”. After that it holds the Fort Dearborn Addition lot sale of June 1839, where the bidder is printed “N. King”; Norris 1844's “King, N. clerk, at T. King's”; and a Fergus 1839 line matched on the initial N which reads, in full, “King, Nathaniel, clerk, Tuthill King”. NATHANIEL IS NOT NEHEMIAH. The directory prints a Nathaniel King clerking for Tuthill King and the 1844 volume prints an N. King doing the same thing in the same shop, so the N. readings have a documented owner who is not this man, and the card is gathering them on an initial — C1's ANDREWS DAVID test, read the field and not the grade. What is left to check the register's three June 1835 rows against is one newspaper printing of a name, with no trade, no street, no office and UNKNOWN in the Residence column. That is one name-only reading and nothing else, which is the shape of eleven of cohort B's twelve refusals. Refused; filed on the way past as the card's own question.

One of the two rows states ILLINOIS in the Residence column and the town-side partner cohort B says that column needs is as good as this dataset holds: Andreas's list of the settlement's residents has “James Kinzie and family ... resided near Wentworth's tavern”, he is a candidate at the first town election of 10 August 1833 and takes five votes, he stood surety on Mark Beaubien's ferry bond, and he built the Green Tree Tavern in 1833 and leased it. The two rows are 80-acre canal entries in section 9 T39N R14E, 28 and 29 September 1830 — the section immediately west of the one Robert A. Kinzie entered, in the quarter of the settlement where this card's own house stands. The register prints JAMES in full and the layer's four Kinzies are James, John Harris, Juliette and Robert Allen, four forenames that cannot be confused; the register itself sells to no second Kinzie but Robert A. THE 1839 DIRECTORY LINE IS NOT USED: “Kinzie, James, real estate agent, North Canal street” is matched `contested` between three residents of 1835 on the J-initial rule, and a contested line cannot corroborate one of three claimants — the JONES WILLARD reasoning. Upheld on the Residence column with its partner, and on a town record that holds this man continuously from before the entries to long after.

THE PURCHASE IS THE ONE THE CARD ALREADY DESCRIBES. ls0059 is the north fractional half of SECTION 10, T39N R14E, 102.29 acres, 7 May 1831, with COOK in the Residence column — and this card's own note, on Charles Butler's letter of 1881, says that Robert A. Kinzie offered Butler and Arthur Bronson his quarter interest in “the north fractional half of Section 10”, the ground Kinzie's Addition was laid out on. A register row that enters the man on exactly the tract the town's history says he held is the strongest form of the check this rule asks for: the document predicts the row rather than merely coinciding with it. The middle initial carries too — the register prints ROBERT A, Fergus 1839 “Kinzie, Robert A., Davis, Kinzie & Hyde, Kinzie street” and Fergus 1843 “Kinzie, Robert Allen” — and the trade arm agrees, a merchant of the 1833 roster and a candidate at the first town election with nine votes. Upheld on all four arms at once; it is the cleanest uphold in the cohort.

A CONTRACTION, NOT A BARER SPELLING — cohort C2's HARMON CHAS L control, and it is what keeps the Brown rule from swallowing this pair. GEO W is George W. abbreviated and it keeps the token that discriminates: Fergus 1839 prints TWO men here, “Merrill, George W., dry goods merchant, 166 Lake st” and “Merrill, George, clerk, Geo. Chacksfield”, and the W is the only thing that separates them. The register prints the W on both of its rows and the directory prints it in 1839 and again in 1843 (“Merrill, George W., provisions, etc., 157 Lake, s.e. cor LaSalle”). Beside the initial the town holds this man in four further documents — the poll list of 1835, the 1840 census, Norris 1844 and the Second Presbyterian history — and the layer's only other Merrill is Winthrop. WHAT IS WEAK HERE AND IS NOT HIDDEN: the earliest town-side reading is the poll of 31 December 1835, which is nine months AFTER this row of 7 March 1836 was entered but is the record's first sight of the man at all, and the card's own present_on_scene_date is `uncertain` for that reason. A ruling on a purchase is not a ruling on residence and does not move that field. Upheld on the middle initial the register repeats.

The full spelling of the pair ruled above, and it goes the same way for the same reason: the middle initial W is printed by the register and by Fergus 1839 and 1843, and it is what separates this man from the “Merrill, George, clerk” the 1839 volume prints four lines away. ls0697 is 80 acres in section 33 T38N R14E entered on 27 June 1835 — the ring's own day, when nearly two hundred rows were written. Ruled separately from MERRILL GEO W because C1's rule is that a spelling is its own proposal; they agree here, where BROWN WILLIAM H and BROWN WM did not, because neither of these spellings has dropped the discriminating token. The same weakness applies and is stated the same way: the town's first sight of the man is the poll of 31 December 1835, six months after this row. Upheld on the middle initial the register repeats and on the four later documents that hold him at one corner of Lake and LaSalle from 1839 to 1844.

A MIDDLE INITIAL ON BOTH SIDES, AND A FIRM THAT NAMES THE OTHER MULFORD. The register enters MULFORD JAMES H for lot 8 of block 119 and lot 8 of block 96 on 25 October 1833, at the town's own school-section sale; Fergus 1839 prints “Mulford, James H. & Edward H. jr., jewelers, etc., Dearborn st” — the forename whole, the middle initial H, and, in the same line, the E. H. Mulford the layer holds as this card's only namesake, which is exactly the discrimination the register's H performs. The town holds the man on the tax list of 1833 — the same year as the two rows — and on the polls of 1834 and 1835, so the civic rolls bracket the entries on both sides, and the Democrat prints him twice besides (“J. H. Mulford”, 4 June 1834; “Mulford, J. H.”, 17 September 1834). Upheld on the middle initial and the bracket together.

THE PRINTED RECORD HOLDS A SECOND JOHN MURPHY AND THE REGISTER'S ROW CANNOT EXCLUDE HIM — the BROWN WM rule, on a surname where it bites hardest. Fergus 1843 prints “Murphy, John, prop. United States Hotel ... alderman 4th ward” AND “Murphy, John, laborer, res North Water near Pine”; Norris 1844 prints both again. The register's ls0581 is bare JOHN MURPHY, 80 acres in section 4 T38N R14E on 4 June 1835, with no middle initial and UNKNOWN in the Residence column, and there is nothing in it that could choose between them. THE CARD IS STRONG AND THAT IS NOT THE QUESTION. This household is, in its own note's words, the best-attested occupancy of a named building in the dataset — Andreas twice, in two chapters, has Mr and Mrs John Murphy taking charge of the Exchange Coffee House in August 1834 and staying to 1836, and the polls of 1834 and 1835 hold him. All of that argues that a John Murphy lived here; none of it argues that THIS John Murphy entered those eighty acres, and a tavern keeper's trade predicts a quarter-section purchase no better than a labourer's does. What the card demonstrates is the thinness the Brown rule was written for: the layer holds one John Murphy because the layer is thin, and the town printed at least two. Refused; eighty acres and $100 come back off the card.

THE TRADE IS ABOUT LAND AND THE REGISTER IS WHAT YOU WOULD PREDICT FROM IT — the PEARSONS and EGAN reasoning, the cheapest uphold in the rule when the directory names a trade about ground. Fergus 1839 prints “Noble, John, real estate, res. Dutchman's Point”, and the register enters him for 320 acres of section 12 T40N R13E on one day, 25 December 1834, in the townships between the town and Dutchman's Point, plus a school-section town lot in October 1833. The Residence column reads COOK on one of the two quarter sections and the town-side partner cohort B requires it to have is the poll list of 1834. Beside that the town holds the man three more times and not as a bare name: the Calumet Club's 1879 reception of settlers prior to 1840, where he gave his own date, and the Fergus 1843 volume's death-notice list. The layer's other Nobles are Mark Esq., Mark's people and William B., and the register itself sells to NOBLE MARK, MARK JR and MARK SEN and to one John only, so the register discriminates its own Nobles by forename. Upheld on the trade arm with the Residence column behind it.

TWO MIDDLE INITIALS, PRINTED ON BOTH SIDES, FOUR TIMES IN THE TOWN'S OWN PAPER. The Democrat has “Thomas J. V. Owen” (24 December 1833), “T. J. V. Owen” (18 June 1834), “Th. J. V. Owen” (2 July 1834) and “Col. T. J. V. Owen” (26 November 1834); the poll list of the first town election prints “Owen, Col. T. J. V.”; the register prints OWEN THOMAS J V. The four rows are whole blocks and town lots at the school-section sale of 23 and 24 October 1833 — $676 in four days — and the buyer is the town's FIRST PRESIDENT, chosen ten weeks earlier with 26 of 28 votes, and the United States' Indian agent, a man whose office and purse the town's own sale is exactly what you would predict him at. Presence is closed at both ends of the entries: Andreas has him arriving in the spring of 1831 and dying at Chicago on 15 October 1835. Upheld on the initials and the office together.

UPHELD ON A SECOND DOCUMENT THAT SAYS SOMETHING, and it is the weakest uphold in the cohort, marked so here. The town holds this man three times: the Democrat prints “Reed, Thomas” on 3 September 1834 in an ordinary printing with its own locator, the poll list of 1835 holds him, and one uncalled-for letter of 20 May 1835 carries the name — C1's test applied, read `press_evidence[].list` and not the flag, and the flag would have been wrong here because only one of the two press rows is a letter list. Fergus 1839 then prints “Reed, Thomas, teamster, 115 Lake street”: a trade AND a street, which is what separates this card from the cohort's refusals, where the second document repeats the name and says nothing further. The entry is 27 June 1835, four days before the scene date and inside the ring. WHAT IS MISSING IS SAID PLAINLY: no middle initial, UNKNOWN in the Residence column, and a teamster's trade predicts an 80-acre entry no better than anybody's. What carries it is that the register sells to REED JAMES W, REED ROBERT and one Thomas, the directory prints one Thomas, and the layer's other Reeds are J. W., George, S. W. and William. Upheld on the second-document arm.

THREE WHOLE BLOCKS FOR $1,205 AGAINST A CARD THAT IS ONE LINE OF A TAX ROLL. The register enters RUSSELL SAMUEL for blocks 90, 86 and 45 at the school-section sale of 23 and 24 October 1833, among the largest single-hand takings of that sale; the card is a G3 PROJECTED RESIDENT — the ladder's own weakest rung — documented once, on the town's tax list of 1833, and corroborated by nothing. No press printing, no poll list, no middle initial, UNKNOWN in the Residence column, `present_on_scene_date` uncertain, and no Samuel Russell printed in Fergus 1839, Fergus 1843 or Norris 1844. That is one name-only reading and nothing else, the shape cohort B refused eleven times. The rule's own words govern: a bare name on each side is refused however unlikely the coincidence looks, and here the coincidence is not even unlikely — the register's biggest buyers at that sale were not all townsmen. Refused; three blocks, 13.58 acres and $1,205.00 come back off the card. The wider question this row and SKINNER JOSEPH raise together — whether buying at the town's OWN school-section sale is itself a check on a town-side name — is filed rather than decided here, because deciding it would change rulings already made.

THE MIDDLE INITIAL IS ON BOTH SIDES AND THE MIDDLE NAME IS PRINTED IN FULL. The Democrat prints “Silas W. Sherman” on 3 December 1833 and “Sherman, Silas W.” on 26 August 1835, Fergus 1839 “Sherman, Silas W., ex-sheriff, 48 Clark street” and Fergus 1843 “Sherman, Silas Wooster, elected sheriff Cook County in 1834 and 1836”; the register prints SHERMAN SILAS W. The two press printings fall on either side of the entry — block 98 at the school-section sale, 24 October 1833 — and the poll of 1834 holds him between them, so the town's own paper brackets the row. He was elected SHERIFF OF COOK COUNTY the year after it. The forename is uncommon, the layer's other Shermans are Mrs H. and Rebecca, and the register's only other is Francis C. Upheld on the middle initial and the bracket.

THE CLOSEST CALL IN THE COHORT, AND THE LINE IT DRAWS IS THE ONE C3 ADDS: a second document must SAY something, not merely repeat the name. The town holds Joseph Skinner twice — the tax list of 1833 and one return of letters uncalled-for at the post office, 1 April 1834 — and NEITHER prints a trade, a street, an office or a middle initial. No directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 prints a Joseph Skinner at all, which is the test cohort A found decided all three of its refusals, and the card's own `present_on_scene_date` is uncertain. Counting to two is not the rule; the rule is that the register's row can be CHECKED against something, and two bare names cannot check a third. What argues the other way is worth stating because it is the reason this is close: the rows are lots 1 and 8 of block 117 at the town's OWN school-section sale of 22 October 1833, and a man on the town's tax list of that same year is the kind of man who bought there. That argument is not one of the rule's four arms and it would, if admitted, reopen rulings already made — so it is FILED as a question rather than used here. Refused; two lots and $212.00 come back off the card.

THE COMMONEST SURNAME IN THE TOWN, A BARE FORENAME, AND THREE PRINTED CLAIMANTS. The register's ls0501 is SMITH GEORGE, 80 acres in section 6 T40N R14E on 27 June 1835 at $2.80 the acre, with UNKNOWN in the Residence column. The card is a coffee-house keeper, minted from the Democrat of 5 November 1834 and 20 May 1835 and holding a trade and nothing else — no street, no household, no civic roll, and `present_on_scene_date` uncertain because the corpus stops six weeks before the scene date. Against that the printed record holds at least three distinct George Smiths: Fergus 1839's “Smith, George W., general merchant, North Water street”, Fergus 1843's “Smith, George (George Smith & Co.) ... bankers and exchange brokers, 1 LaSalle”, and Norris 1844's two entries for the banking house. The layer holds ELEVEN Smiths, and the register sells to eleven spellings of the surname. A coffee-house keeper's trade predicts no quarter-section, the bare forename excludes nobody, and upholding this would put a speculator's entry on the card of the one George Smith in the town whose record contains no land at all. Refused; eighty acres and $224.00 come back off the card.

THE MIRROR OF SMITH GEORGE, ON THE SAME SURNAME AND THE SAME DAY OF THE RING, AND IT GOES THE OTHER WAY — which is the point. What refused George Smith was a second printed man of the forename; there is no second Jeremiah Smith anywhere in this corpus. Fergus 1839's J-Smiths are James M., John E., John M., John L., Dr John Mark and Joseph F.; Norris 1844's are J. A., J. F. and J. T.; no volume prints a Jeremiah. The layer holds eleven Smiths and one Jeremiah, and the register — which sells to SMITH J, JEBUTHOM, JEDUTHAN, JEDUTHOM, JEDUTHON, JOSHUA, LIMAN, SIMAN, WILLIAM and GEORGE besides — sells to one JEREMIAH, four times. TWO OF THOSE FOUR ROWS STATE COOK IN THE RESIDENCE COLUMN, and the town-side partner cohort B requires is a Black Hawk War enrolment at Chicago in 1832 and the Democrat printing the forename in full, “Jeremiah Smith”, on 24 December 1834 — ten weeks after the first two rows and six months before the last. The town's paper and the muster roll bracket the entries on both sides. Upheld on the Residence column with its partner, on an uncommon forename printed whole on both sides of a common surname.

THE TOWN'S OWN SURVEYOR AND ASSESSOR, BUYING AT THE TOWN'S OWN SALE SIX WEEKS BEFORE IT APPOINTED HIM. The register enters SNOW GEORGE W for blocks 55 and 46 at the school-section sale of 24 October 1833; the first board of trustees made George W. Snow the town's Assessor and Surveyor on 4 December 1833, and he was one of the twelve who voted for incorporation on 5 August 1833 and one of the twenty-eight electors five days later. The middle initial is on both sides and the middle NAME is printed: the Democrat's “G. W. Snow” of 18 June 1834, Fergus 1843's “Snow, George Washington, lumber merchant”, Norris 1844's “Snow, G. W. lumber merchant, South Water st”. The tax list of 1833 and the poll of 1834 bracket the rows, Andreas's roster has “George W. Snow, came in 1832”, and the layer's only other Snow is Watson M. A LATER TRADE THAT AGREES: a lumber merchant of 1843 is a plausible town-lot buyer of 1833, but the ruling does not rest on 1843 — it rests on the initial, the bracket and the office. Upheld.

THE MIDDLE INITIAL IS ON BOTH SIDES AND THE FORENAME IS UNIQUE AMONG SEVEN TAYLORS. The register prints TAYLOR ANSON H once, 160 acres in section 30 T40N R14E on 8 June 1835; Fergus 1839 prints “Taylor, Anson H[.], general supply store, near the Garrison”, the volume's only Anson, its other A-Taylors being Andrew and Augustin Deodat. Andreas has “Anson H. and his brother, Charles Taylor, came in 1832” and credits him with the log bridge across the South Branch that was, before 1834, the only bridge teams could cross; the poll lists and the 1832 militia enrolment hold him. A CAUTION THAT THIS RULING DOES NOT RESOLVE AND MUST NOT HIDE: the card's own press reading is “Anson W. Taylor”, 12 November 1834, and its research note records an “A. W. Taylor” on the 1832 militia roll — a middle initial that disagrees with everything else on the card. Whether the card is gathering an Anson W. beside its Anson H. is a card question, filed on the way past; it does not touch the register's row, which prints H as the directory does. Upheld on the middle initial.

THE BROTHER ABOVE IS UPHELD AND THIS ONE IS REFUSED, OFF THE SAME CARD, FOR THE REASON C2 NAMED: ask whether the token that discriminates is missing. The card is CHARLES H. Taylor; the register prints CHARLES bare on all five rows. And the printed record holds two of him — Fergus 1839's “Taylor, Charles, tailor, Clark street” AND “Taylor, Charles H., tailor, Francis H. Taylor”; Fergus 1843's “Taylor, Charles, merchant tailor, 42 Clark ... alderman 3d ward” AND “Taylor, Charles H., currier”; Norris 1844 the same pair again. The card's own research note is the warning: this parcel's sources carry at least four Taylors plus the “Charles and Mary Taylor” of the Wolf Point tavern, and no two of them are merged, because merging on a surname is how a documented population quietly becomes a fictional one. THE RESIDENCE COLUMN CANNOT RESCUE IT, and this is the refinement the row adds to cohort B's arm: ls0015 states COOK and the poll lists of 1833, 1834 and 1835 are a town-side partner, but BOTH printed Charles Taylors are Chicago men, so a county name chooses between them no better than the bare forename does. Refused; five rows, 324 acres and $993.60 come back off the card.

THE MIDDLE INITIAL IS ON BOTH SIDES AND THE DEMOCRAT BRACKETS THE DAY. The paper prints “Edmund D. Taylor” on 25 March 1835 and “E. D. Taylor” on 8 July 1835; the four register rows are all 27 June 1835, between them — 368 acres across three townships for $612 in one afternoon of the ring. Fergus 1839 prints “Taylor, Col. Edmund D., Taylor, Breese Co., Lake street”, a named firm, and the volume's other E-Taylor is Ezra; Norris 1844 has “Taylor, E. coffee house, South Water st”, and the Calumet Club's 1879 reception of settlers prior to 1840 holds him. EDMUND is the only one of the seven Taylors in the layer to bear that forename and the register sells to one. A man of a Lake Street firm taking four tracts on the ring's busiest day is what the second-document arm was written for. Upheld on the middle initial with the bracket behind it.

EIGHT WHOLE BLOCKS AT THE TOWN'S OWN SALE, BY A MAN THE TOWN HAD ALREADY WATCHED PUT $100 INTO A BUILDING. Andreas: “Dr. John T. Temple, who had arrived early in July, 1833, with his family ... came to Chicago from Washington, D. C., armed with a contract to carry the mails from Chicago to Fort Howard, Green Bay”, and he then headed the subscription for the Temple Building with $100. The register enters TEMPLE JOHN T for blocks 99, 112, 76, 77, 111, 110, 17 and 103 on 22, 23 and 24 October 1833, $1,107 in three days, eleven weeks after he arrived. The middle initial is on both sides and the middle name is printed in full: the poll of the first town election prints “Temple, John T.”, the tax list of 1833 “Temple, John”, the poll of 1834 “Temple, John T.”, the Democrat “Dr. J. T. Temple” (3 December 1833), Fergus 1839 “Temple, Dr. John T., 218 Lake st” and Fergus 1843 “Temple, John Taylor, physician, 218 Lake”. The rolls of 1833 stand on both sides of the rows. The layer's other Temples are Mrs Temple and Dr Peter Temple. Upheld on every arm the rule has.

THE REGISTER'S OWN MIDDLE INITIAL POINTS AT A RIVAL CARD, NOT AT THIS ONE. The register prints THOMPSON JOHN L; the card it was matched to is “John Thompson”, which carries no middle initial at all, while the layer holds `thompson_lieut_j_l`, “Lieut J L Thompson”, whose initials are exactly the register's. The mechanical rule matched on the forename and could not see that the discriminating token belongs to somebody else. That alone would be enough. The card is also the weakest kind this project keeps: `letter_list_ only` is TRUE and it is true — C1's test applied, read `press_evidence[].list` and not the flag, and the only press row IS a return of uncalled-for letters, printed “Thompaon” and “Thompsond, John” in the Democrat of 4 March 1834 and 20 May 1835. No trade, no street, no civic roll, no directory line, UNKNOWN in the Residence column, and `present_on_scene_date` uncertain. The one book reading on the card, the 1843 volume's death notice for “Thompson, Gen. John Leverett” who died in 1888, is a second thing the initial L appears to have dragged in. Refused; two rows, 161.31 acres and $201.63 come back off the card. Whether the L is the Lieutenant's is filed, not decided.

A MIDDLE INITIAL DISCRIMINATES; IT DOES NOT CORROBORATE — cohort B's ROWLEY HEMAN A and HURD NIRAM F, exactly. The card is a G3 PROJECTED RESIDENT whose entire record is ONE return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office, the Democrat of 20 May 1835, read through bad type as “'fucker, Alexr. H. ot”. `letter_list_only` is true and correct. The register's ls0531 is 160 acres in section 18 T40N R14E on 27 June 1835 with UNKNOWN in the Residence column. The H agrees on both sides and that agreement IS the town's whole record: there is nothing else to check — no trade, no street, no civic roll, no directory line in 1839, 1843 or 1844, and the resident-research corpus records a documented no-find. An uncalled-for letter says a correspondent thought the name reachable at Chicago; a tract entry says a name entered ground; the rule refuses the pair. Refused; 160 acres and $200.00 come back off the card.

THE REGISTER ITSELF PROVES THE SECOND MAN, and that is the lesson this cohort adds to the Brown rule: the discriminating evidence need not be in the town's printed record when the REGISTER discriminates on its own paper. It sells to WENTWORTH ELIJAH, WENTWORTH ELIJAH SEN, WENTWORTH ELIJAH W and WENTWORTH ELIJAM SEN — at least two Elijah Wentworths, a senior and one who is not, and this layer holds ONE, with no middle initial and no “Sen”. A card that can meet none of the register's own distinctions cannot be given a row the register took the trouble to distinguish. The town's side is thin besides: the only contemporary reading is “E. Wentworth”, Democrat of 7 January 1834 — an INITIAL, which the layer's own H. E. Wentworth answers to as readily — and the forename is printed whole only in an 1863 death notice and the census of 1840. No trade, no street, no civic roll, no directory line, UNKNOWN in the Residence column. Refused; eighty acres and $100.00 come back off the card.

THE SAME SURNAME'S OTHER SPELLING, REFUSED FOR THE SHARPER FORM OF THE SAME REASON. Where the bare ELIJAH could not meet the register's own SEN, this one carries a middle initial W THAT THE CARD DOES NOT HAVE AND THAT NOTHING ON THE TOWN'S SIDE EVER PRINTS — not the Democrat's “E. Wentworth”, not the 1863 death notice, not the 1840 census. C2's control cuts the other way here: HARMON CHAS L was upheld because a CONTRACTION keeps the token that discriminates, and an ADDED initial is not a contraction, it is a discriminator the card cannot meet. The register's own WENTWORTH ZEBIAH W, twice, shows the W is a family's initial and not a stray. ls0892 is 80 acres in section 10 T40N R13E on 18 November 1834, UNKNOWN in the Residence column. Refused; eighty acres and $100.00 come back off the card. The corpus carries twenty Wilsons, among them a John C., a John Lush, a John McNeil, a John Quintard and a 'W S Wilson', so the S has somewhere else to land inside the surname. T-0700 refused WILSON JOHN L against this same one card for the same want of a discriminator, and T-1033 records that the rule has since caught up with that spelling on its own. Lots 9 and 10 of block 6, 28 June 1836, $3,690, retracted.

UPHELD, and it is the cohort's demonstration that a namesake is only a rival where the printed record can hold one. The layer's three Baileys are Amos, Bennet and Esth[er] R. M., so the mechanical rule chose on the forename alone; the test is not the layer but the page, and the page is not thin here. The three directories print SIX Baileys between them — Amos, Bennett, Henry and Joseph in Fergus 1839; Harlow and Justice added by Fergus 1843 and Norris 1844 — and exactly one of the six is an Amos: 'Bailey, Amos, carpenter and surveyor' (f1839_e0041, printed page 6), printed in 1839 and in neither later book. The Democrat and the American, which print Bennet Bailey twice in the 1835 letter lists, a Samuel J., an Esther M., a James and an H. W., print no Amos Bailey at all. So the forename is a discriminating token against the FULLEST record the town has, which is what BROWN WM asks and what BROWN WM did not have. The second limb is the trade: the directories crosswalk already matches f1839_e0041 to this person with `could_carry: [occupation]`, so the town holds a carpenter and surveyor of this name and not a bare one, and two town lots at the June 1836 sale is a purchase a building tradesman in that month is consistent with. Lot 5 of block 16 and lot 6 of block 5, 28 and 30 June 1836, $3,720, stand. The 1839 trade has not been SPENT onto the card — that is T-0987's work and not a ruling's.

REFUSED, and the two initials are not the discriminator they look like. The town's whole record of an L. B. Cobb is ONE line — 'Cobb, L. B.' in the 1835 poll list — and the register's 'COBB L B' is the second bare name; the ruling rule calls that two name-only readings and not an identity. What makes the refusal positive rather than an admission of thinness is the Cobb the town DOES document, and he carries the same middle initial: S. B. Cobb, saddle, harness and trunk manufactory at the corner of Lake street, advertised in the American of 8 and 13 June 1835 out of the dissolution of Goss & Cobb, a 'Silas Cobb' in the Democrat's letter list of 1 April 1834, and 'Cobb, Silas B.' at 171 Lake in Fergus 1839 and 'Silas Bowman' in Norris 1844. Beside him the directories print one other Cobb, Geo. W., a clerk. So the B does not choose between the proposal and its namesake — both have it — and the only thing that does is the forename initial, read once on each side and printed nowhere else in the corpus. A $9,000 lot (lot 2 of block 33, 21 June 1836) is a large thing to hang on a single letter that no second document repeats. Retracted.

REFUSED, and it is the cohort's largest retraction by rows. The card looks like three domains and is one reading: 'Foster, Amos' in the 1833 poll list. Its two directory readings are 'Foster, A. H. (Jennings & F.)' (Fergus 1843) and 'Foster, A. H. of Jennings & F.' (Norris 1844), folded on by the crosswalk's forename rule — 'the given name of both begins A' — which is agreement on one letter and disagreement on the H that follows it; A. H. Foster boards the American Temperance House in both years and is a partner in Jennings & Foster, and nothing ties him to an Amos. Strip that fold and the printed record holds NO Amos Foster anywhere: Fergus 1839 and 1843 and Norris 1844 give Dr. John Herbert, Edward, George Franklin and A. H.; the Democrat's letter lists of 1834 and 1835 give Caleb four times, Alburn, Jacob P. and a J. H. So the proposal is a poll line of 1833 against twenty-five register rows of 27 and 28 September 1830 — the first sale of the town, three years EARLIER than the one reading — with UNKNOWN in the Residence column. Two name-only readings, and the earlier one is the register's own. Twenty-five rows and $468 retracted.

UPHELD on a trade and a premises printed three weeks before the scene date. The Democrat of 10 June 1835 carries James Grant's own professional card — 'JAMES GRANT, attorney and counsellor at law', office in the store of Hubbard & Co., La Salle Street — one of four new Chicago houses advertising in that issue, and the anchor claim for the brick store it stands in. Fergus 1839 prints him again in the same trade and a different house, 'Grant, Jas., attorney, N. Water st near Rush, bds. Lake House', and the old-settler death notices carry 'Grant, James', 14 March 1891. The layer's one rival is Thomas D. Grant and the printed record adds no second James, so the forename discriminates on the page and not merely in a thin layer. Eleven lots of blocks 2, 4, 5 and 6, 28 June 1836, $28,120 — a speculation in the boom month by a lawyer with an office in it — stand. ONE CAUTION RECORDED RATHER THAN ACTED ON: the card also carries 'J. GRANT, Jr.', regimental adjutant of the Cook county regiment, from the Democrat of 3 September 1834, and a 'Jr.' is the one suffix that says the town held two men of a name. That fold was made on an initial and a suffix; it is a card-merge question, not a purchaser question, and the register prints JAMES in full.

UPHELD, and this is the pair of initials doing what COBB L B's could not. Six Hubbards stand in the layer — Ahira, B., Elijah Kent, Gurdon Saltonstall, Henry G. and Otis — and the printed record adds Moses and Thomas R. and still holds exactly one H. G.: 'Hubbard, Henry G., at G. S. Hubbard & Co.'s warehouse' (Fergus 1839), 'Hubbard, Henry George, clerk, Circuit Court' (Fergus 1843), 'Hubbard, H. G. at clerk's office' (Norris 1844). The town prints the register's own abbreviation, and prints it beside the men it is not: G. S., E. K., A. So the initials are checked against the fullest record and not against a gap. Behind them is a standing: the Democrat of 2 July 1834 sets Henry G. Hubbard as a proprietor of Hubbard & Co., commission and forwarding merchants, and the issue of 5 August 1835 sets 'Moxa Go Hornage' — read Hubbard, [Henry] G. — as a partner of the house beside Gurdon S. Hubbard. A partner in the town's principal forwarding house taking ten lots in blocks 9, 10 and 16 on 29 and 30 June 1836 for $14,720 is a purchase consistent with what is recorded of him, which is the ruling rule's second limb. Stands.

UPHELD, and it is the ruling that says what an initial-only spelling has to survive. A bare H is the BROWN WM shape until you ask the page how many men it could be, and here the page answers: Fergus 1839 prints SIX Hugunins — Capt. Robert, Daniel the ship chandler, Hiram the merchant on West Water street near Lake, James R., John C. and Leonard C. — and exactly one of them begins with H. The town then prints the register's own abbreviation for him: the Democrat of 20 May 1835 sets 'H. HUGUNIN' as chairman of the town meeting, and the corpus reads it Hiram Hugunin because the same run prints him in full as 'Capt. HIRAM HUGUNIN, Agent, Chicago' for the North Western Fire and Marine of Oswego a month later. An initial the town itself uses for one man, unique in the fullest printed record of the surname, is a discriminating token and not the absence of one. The 1835 poll list has 'Hugunin, H.' likewise. Lot 7 of block 23, 24 June 1836, $4,190, stands.

UPHELD, ruled beside HUGUNIN H and for more than that spelling had. The town holds Hiram Hugunin with a trade, an office and a title before the scene date: chairman of the town meeting of 20 May 1835 (Democrat), 'Capt. HIRAM HUGUNIN, Agent, Chicago' for the North Western Fire and Marine Insurance Company of Oswego in the issue of 17 June 1835, writing fire and marine risks; 'Hugunin, Hiram, merchant, West Water street near Lake st' in Fergus 1839; and the old-settler death notices give his death, 12 December 1866. The layer's rival is his namesake Leonard C. Hugunin, himself documented — the letter lists of 31 March and 1 July 1835 and Fergus 1839's 'speculator' — so the forenames are two real men and the register writes one of them in full. Lot 2 of block 31, 21 June 1836, $9,000, stands.

UPHELD, and the eight-strong rival list is the weakest of the cohort once the page is read. The layer's other Kings are Byra, Byram, Byron, Hyram, John Lyle, Nehemiah and Sherman; the three directories print THIRTEEN distinct Kings between them — Byram, Henry, Joe, Joseph, Nathaniel, Richard, Tuthill, Willis and John jr. in Fergus 1839, with J. the carpenter, Solomon, Thomas and Wendell R. added by Fergus 1843 and Norris 1844 — and exactly one of the thirteen is a Tuthill. He is not a name but a shop: the Chicago American of 20 June, 27 June, 4 and 11 July 1835 carries his clothing store, placed three doors north of the Tremont House in Dearborn street, one of the run's first recoverable frontages; Fergus 1839 prints 'King, Tuthill, New York clothing store, 115 Lake st' and Fergus 1843 and Norris 1844 the same trade at the same number. A forename unique in the printed record, on a man with a trade and a premises in the town's own paper in the month of the scene. The two rows are the north and south halves of lot 5 of block 9, both $1,310 on 29 June 1836, which is one parcel bought in halves by one buyer and not the shared-row shape T-1039 described. Stands.

REFUSED, and this project has already refused the identical name once. The register prints JOHN bare on all seven rows of 27 September 1830 with UNKNOWN in the Residence column, and a bare John Kinzie is the one Chicago name of 1830 that cannot be read off the layer: the printed record holds John Harris Kinzie, register of the U.S. land office, AND 'Kinzie, John Harris, jr., killed, Ft. St. Charles, Ark., June 18, 1862, a. 33' (Fergus 1843), AND the elder John Kinzie of Hubbard's own pages. T-0501 met this exact string in McIlvaine's list of the trustees elected 11 August 1834 and REFUSED it — 'the printed name is impossible for the man it looks like and ambiguous among the men it could be' — saying in terms that the identification is probable and was not that pass's to make. THE ARGUMENT THAT WOULD OVERTURN IT IS AVAILABLE AND IS NOT TAKEN, and it is recorded so a later run can weigh it rather than rediscover it: the elder died in 1828 and cannot buy in 1830, and the junior's printed age puts him at about one year old that September, so chronology leaves only John Harris. That is elimination, not a token on the page; the register supplies no middle initial, no trade and no residence, and HARMON ISAAC declined the same shape of argument for the same reason. Consistency between two domains reading one name is worth more here than seven lots. Seven rows of the first town sale and $129 retracted.

REFUSED, and the middle initial the town does hold for a George Lee is the WRONG ONE. The register enters LEE GEORGE W seven times in the June 1836 town sale, and the card it is proposed onto carries exactly three readings: the Democrat's list of letters remaining in the Post Office at Chicago on 20 May 1835, which prints 'George Lee' and nothing else about him and which the newspapers layer itself flags letter_list_only; the residents card built from it; and one St. Cyr marriage of 1 October 1835 signed 'G. S. Lee', folded on by the forename initial alone. So the only middle initial anywhere on the card reads S, against the register's W. The printed record of the surname does not repair it: Fergus 1839, Fergus 1843 and Norris 1844 between them print Benjamin Tyler, Daniel, Daniel J., David S., David Stewart, John and Thomas Lee, and no George at all, and the first city election of 2 May 1837 polls no Lee in any ward. An uncalled-for letter and a tract entry are two name-only readings and do not make an identity (the_ruling_rule), and here they do not even agree on the man's initials. NOTED FOR A LATER RUN, not acted on: whether 'G. S. Lee' belongs on this card at all is a separate question from this ruling, and refusing the purchase does not answer it.

REFUSED on the STANLEY JOSEPH shape, which cohort B drew and this cohort does not bend. The whole of what the town holds for a William Lee is one line of the 1833 tax list, 'Lee, William' (tax_1833_065), with no trade, no address and no second document; the residents card is that line. The register's three rows are lots 5, 6 and 7 of block 23 entered on 28 September 1830 at $25, $25 and $30 — the original canal-commissioners' sale, three years BEFORE the tax line, and a sale whose purchasers were very largely not living here. The printed record adds nothing: no William Lee appears in Fergus 1839, Fergus 1843 or Norris 1844, and the 1837 city poll has no Lee. One civic line against a bare register name is the layer being thin, not the two records agreeing.

REFUSED, and the rival is in the same volume — cohort B's PEARSON HIRAM shape, found a second time. The register itself enters LOOMIS HORATIO G (ls0595, the west half of the south-east quarter, 80 acres at $208, 27 June 1835) a year before the five town lots it enters as LOOMIS H G, so the book holds both spellings of one man, and the H G it is asked about is the man it elsewhere spells out. The printed record of the surname holds exactly two Chicago Loomises and separates them cleanly: 'Loomis, Henry, lumber merchant, cor West Water and Randolph' (Fergus 1843, Norris 1844), who carries NO middle initial in any printing; and Horatio Gates Loomis of Harmon & Loomis, printed 'Loomis, Horatio G., (Harmon & Loomis)' and 'Loomis, Horatio Gates, at C. L. Harmon's' in Fergus 1839 and 1843 and 'Loomis, H. G. at C. L. Harmon's' in Norris 1844 — the register's two initials exactly. The one 1835 reading on the Henry card is weaker still and cannot decide anything: 'H. Loomis' is a signature on the passengers' card of the steamboat Thomas Jefferson printed by the Chicago American of 20 June 1835, an initial that fits either man, and the signer gives BALLSTON SPA as his own place. The residents layer holds no card for Horatio Gates Loomis, so there is no person here to name the rows onto; the ruling refuses the match and records whose rows they are.

REFUSED, on the commonest surname in the cohort and the thinnest card under it. What the town holds for a George Miller is one line of the 1833 tax list (tax_1833_073) and the residents card made from it — no trade, no address, no second reading. Against that, the surname is printed as often as any in the town and never with this forename: Fergus 1839, Fergus 1843 and Norris 1844 print Bernhart, Capt. Harry, Charles/Chas., Daniel, David, H., Henry, Jacob, John, John Newhouse, Peter, Porter, Robert, S. T. and William Miller, and the Democrat and the American between 1833 and 1835 print eighteen more readings of the surname — Chas., Col. Samuel, Daniel, F. W., Henry F., Jacob, Jacob V., Jesse, Jesse F., John, Lorin, Marshall, Matthias B., Samuel and an uncertain L. P. — with no George among them. Nor does the 1837 city poll: its only Millers are Daniel and John B. The three rows are lot 8 of block 18 and lots 5 and 6 of block 36, all entered 27 September 1830 at $25, $36 and $27 — the original sale again, and thirty-three months before the tax line. A bare name in a register and a bare name on a tax roll do not make an identity.

REFUSED — the BROWN WM shape at its plainest, and the cohort's clearest case that an initial is not a forename. The register prints a single letter, J, on two lots of the June 1836 town sale (lot 3 of block 41, $1,125, and lot 8 of block 38, $1,166), and the printed record of the surname holds at least four distinct men whose forename begins with it: Jacob Miller the blacksmith of Indiana Street and Jacob V. Miller (Fergus 1843, Norris 1844, the Democrat, the old-settler death notices), Jesse F. Miller (Democrat, 19 August 1835), Jonathan Miller (St. Cyr, 1838) and John Miller, with a John Newhouse Miller and a John B. Miller besides. The mechanical rule reached miller_john only because the residents layer is thinner than the town was. That card is itself name-only in every one of its readings — poll_1833_020, tax_1833_074, poll_1834_072 and two Democrat readings, one of them a letter list — so even if the initial could be made to choose, there would be nothing on the far side to check the register against.

REFUSED, and the reading that made the card look thick belongs to another town. miller_samuel carries five readings, and on the face of it two of them are newspaper readings that are not letter lists — 'Col. Samuel Miller' in the Democrat of 25 February 1834 and 'Samuel Miller' on 4 March 1834, the second carrying the occupation 'agent'. Read at the page they are ONE advertisement printed twice, David Carver's storage, commission and lumber notice, and its closing sentence is 'Calvin Britain esq. at St. Joseph, and Col. Samuel Miller, Michigan City, are his Agents, who will immediately forward any article directed to him.' The Colonel is Carver's agent at MICHIGAN CITY, Indiana — named in a Chicago paper because Chicago readers shipped through him, not because he lived here. Strip that fold and what remains for a Chicago Samuel Miller is two bare names: tax_1833_075 and an 1832 Black Hawk enrollment (blackhawk_1832_070), neither with a trade, an address or a second document. The register's four rows are lots 3, 4, 5 and 6 of block 14 entered 27 September 1830 at $20, $20, $40 and $30 — the original sale, two years before the muster. No Samuel Miller is printed in Fergus 1839, Fergus 1843 or Norris 1844. Two name-only readings do not make an identity, and a third that turns out to name an Indiana man makes it worse rather than better. The fold itself — a Michigan City agent's two readings sitting on a Chicago resident card — is filed as T-1040 rather than repaired here: a ruling refuses a purchase and does not rewrite a card.

UPHELD, and the register sorts its own Montgomerys before the town is asked. The book holds four spellings: MONTGOMERY LOTON WM and MONTGOMERY LOTON W, both already upheld to the shoemaker Loton W. Montgomery under T-0990; MONTGOMERY JOHN, whose Residence column reads MCLEAN; and the five town lots of 1836 entered as WILLIAM. So the man who signs 'L. W. MONTGOMERY' in the Democrat is in the register under his own forename and is not the purchaser here. The printed record then holds exactly one Chicago Montgomery whose forename begins with W, and prints it out: 'Wm. Montgomery' votes in the First Ward at the first city election of 2 May 1837 (Fergus 1839), the only Montgomery polled in the whole book. His trade is what the rows are: the Democrat carries 'W. MONTGOMERY' ten times between 28 January 1834 and 12 August 1835, signing as auctioneer ('W. MONTGOMERY, Auc’r.'), as agent and as a commission merchant on South Water Street, and the American of 4 July 1835 carries him too — a land agent and auctioneer is exactly the man who takes lots 1, 2, 4 and 9 of blocks 12 and 13 in the June 1836 sale and lot 8 of block 30 that September, $13,850 in all. The layer's other Montgomerys, G. B. S. the shoemaker and J. H. the shipcarpenter, are printed distinctly in both directories and take neither the initial nor the trade. FILED ON THE WAY PAST as T-1040, and not folded into this ruling: the newspapers gazetteer's person_w_montgomery carries 'boot and shoe maker' among its occupations, which is Loton W.'s trade and not this man's — the two signatures are separated on the page and should be on the card.

UPHELD, and it is the least doubtful ruling of the cohort. The register's two initials, B and S, are the two initials the town itself prints: the Democrat of 17 June 1835 has 'B. S. Morris', the same run carries the firm 'Casey & Morris, attorneys at law' on 26 August 1835, Fergus 1843 prints both the entry 'Morris, Buckner Smith, attorney, 59 Clark, res Indiana, bet Cass and Rush' and his own advertising card 'B. S. MORRIS, attorney and counsellor at law, office Clark Street, opposite City Hotel', and Norris 1844 repeats the card. Buckner Smith Morris is the town's second mayor and the corpus holds him with a trade, an office and a house. The surname has no rival that could take a B: the layer's other Morrises are Ann and Mary, from the church register and the 1840 census, and Potily, a St. Cyr marriage of 1835. The register enters MORRIS B S once — lot 2 of block 2 on 5 September 1836, $1,900 — and no other Morris at all in seven townships. Both initials agreeing, a trade in the scene year, and no rival reading anywhere in the surname.

UPHELD on the two-initial agreement, which the one-initial refusals in this same cohort throw into relief. The register prints J M, and the town prints J. M.: the poll of 1834 enters 'Morrison, J. M.' (poll_1834_075), letter for letter the register's spelling, and Fergus 1843 and Norris 1844 both carry 'Morrison, James M., carpenter' on Clark Street near Madison, with the 1840 census reading 'Jam[e]s [?] Morrison' on the same card. Four domains, a trade and an address. The surname is populous and that is the point: Fergus 1839, Fergus 1843 and Norris 1844 print Alexander, Charles, Daniel, Ephraim (and Eph. and Ephriam), Ezekiel, James M., John C., Michael and Orsemus Morrison, and only ONE of them carries M as a middle initial. The register sorts them too — it enters EZEKIEL, ORSEMUS three times, EPHRAIM and THOS M under their own names, so J M is not a clipped reading of a purchaser the book holds otherwise. Two lots of the June 1836 town sale, lot 1 of block 38 at $7,800 and lot 6 of block 57 at $2,020. The price is large for a carpenter and is not an argument either way: the ruling is about which man the letters name, and $9,820 in the week of the town sale says nothing about a trade.

REFUSED, and the middle initial is what refuses it rather than what carries it. The card `smith_james` holds no middle initial of its own: its one scene-window reading is `chicago_american_1835_06_20#c011`, the passengers' CARD of the steamboat Thomas Jefferson on her trip from Buffalo, sixty-three signatures each giving the place its signer calls his own, and the transcription reads the line 'Janes Stmth'. A signature on a boat's card of thanks is a name and nothing else, and it is not even a statement that the signer stayed. What the directories add is a fold, not a man: Fergus 1843 and Norris 1844 are both recorded AMBIGUOUS on this card — four printed entries (James the shoemaker at David Jay's, James Ayer the clerk at L. P. Sanger & Co., J. F. of Skinner & S., J. T. the auctioneer) meet it on 'the given name of both begins J', and the layer holds eleven Smiths. The ONE unambiguous entry the card carries goes the other way: Fergus 1839's single match is 'Smith, James M., constable, Lake street' — M where the register prints A, which is cohort C2's LEE GEORGE W shape exactly, a middle initial that DISAGREES rather than one that is absent. And the printed record's actual James A. Smith is somebody else: 'Smith, James Ayer, clerk' in Fergus 1843, 'Smith, J. A.' in Norris 1844, one of the four entries the fold could not choose among and a person the layer does not hold apart. The register is no help either — the same book enters SMITH J twice beside SMITH JAMES A's three rows, so it is not fastidious about which Smith it is naming. Three rows, $6,275: lot 3 of block 37 at $4,500 on 5 September 1836, and the two halves of lot 4 of block 5 at $887.50 apiece on 28 June. The proposal rests on the residents layer holding one card called 'James Smith', which is the layer being coarse under the commonest surname in the corpus, not two records agreeing. THE ONE FACT THAT CUTS THE OTHER WAY, SAID OUT LOUD: the 1840 federal census of Chicago does carry a head printed “James A. Smith” (33SQ-GYYJ-93G, printed page 207, line 23), and this card holds it — as a CANDIDATE under rule L7, because the name agrees and nothing independent of the name was found. It is not a token: it is the same string arriving a second time, five years after the scene and four after the purchase, and the census crosswalk has already declined to make an identity of it. A candidate on one side and a register row on the other are still two name-only readings. If that head is ever tied to a person by something other than his name, this refusal is the first ruling to revisit.

UPHELD on the strongest thing an initial-only card can be handed: the register prints the forename the card is missing. The layer holds him as 'R. Stewart' and Fergus 1839 prints 'Stewart, Royal, attorney at law, Lake street' — the register's ROYAL in full, with a trade and a street. The printed record of the surname carries four Stewarts in 1839 (Ephriam T. and Hart L. the canal contractors, Capt. John of the steamer Michigan, and Royal) and exactly one Royal; Fergus 1843 and Norris 1844 add E. A./K. A. the watchmaker and repeat Ephraim T. and Hart L., and still no second Royal. The card carries `attorney` as its 1835 trade off the Democrat and the American, so the town holds him in an occupation before the sale as well as after it. The register holds no other Stewart at all in seven townships, so this is not a clipped reading of a purchaser the book already has — C2's first test, and it passes. The layer's only rival is James Stewart, a voter-list and church-roll name, and Royal is not James. Seven lots of the June 1836 town sale, $47,560, the largest single purchaser in this cohort; as C2 wrote of MORRISON J M, the sum says nothing about the trade and the ruling is about which man the letters name.

UPHELD, and rule 2 is live here rather than academic — it just falls the other way. Augustine Deodat Taylor is the carpenter who framed St. Mary's, and the directories print his forenames out in full on their own: 'Taylor, Augustin Deodat, carpenter and builder, 74 Lake st' in Fergus 1839 and 'Taylor, Augustine Deodat, carpenter and builder, res Michigan ave, bet Lake and Randolph' in Fergus 1843, both recorded as single, uncontested entries. Norris 1844 then prints the register's own two letters — 'Taylor, A. D. builder, house Michigan ave. b Lake and Randolph' — at Fergus 1843's address for Augustine, letter for letter. The rival the layer flags is Anson H. Taylor, and his middle initial is H against the register's D; more than that, the register enters him UNDER HIS OWN NAME, TAYLOR ANSON H, one row. Ask the book first and it answers: it sorts its Taylors carefully, entering ANSON H, CHARLES, E D, EDMUND D, SOL, SOLOMON, W H, WILLIAM and WILLIAM H as separate spellings, so A D is not a clipped reading of a Taylor it already holds. Two initials agreeing, a trade the town prints three times, and a rival the register itself keeps apart. Two lots, $5,430 — lot 2 of block 42 on 23 June 1836 and lot 8 of block 6 on the 28th.

UPHELD on both initials, printed in the scene year with a sentence around them. The Democrat of 1 July 1835 reports the Democratic meeting at the Eagle Coffee House on 29 June and names 'S. G. Trowbridge' to the committee of fourteen — the register's two letters exactly, four days before the scene date, in a town meeting rather than a list of names. Fergus 1839 then prints 'Trowbridge, Samuel G., mail contractor, Clark street', which expands the S and keeps the G, and gives him a trade and a street. The printed record of the surname is one line deep: that single 1839 entry is the ONLY Trowbridge in Fergus 1839, Fergus 1843 and Norris 1844 together, so there is no rival reading anywhere rather than none in a thin layer — cohort B's WELLMAKER JOHN distinction. The layer's rival G G Trowbridge differs on the FORENAME initial, not the middle one, and is a voter-list name carrying nothing else. The register enters TROWBRIDGE S G twice and no other Trowbridge: lots 2 and 3 of block 57 on 24 June 1836, $2,750 apiece, adjacent lots on one day.

UPHELD, and ruled together with WALKER GEORGE H because the two spellings are the two forms the town itself prints of one man. The Democrat's letter list of 1 April 1834 prints 'G. H. Walker', which is this spelling letter for letter; Gholson Kercheval's Black Hawk War company roll of 1832 enters him 'WALKER, GEORGE H' as a private, which is the other spelling letter for letter and is a second document with a unit and a rank in it rather than a bare name. The middle initial H is therefore repeated across two independent records and the register's two rows, which is the first thing the ruling rule asks for. The rival is George E. Walker, and rule 2 refuses him: his middle initial is E, and his own card is `letter_list_only` — the Democrat's list of 2 July 1834 and an old-settler death notice of 1874. The sequence argument cohort A used stands behind this one: WALKER G H takes lot 6 of block 37 and WALKER GEORGE H lot 1 of the same block on the same day, 22 June 1836, so the book is entering one buyer's two lots under two spellings of his name on one page. And the printed directories hold no George Walker of either initial at all — Almond, Amos E., Charles, Curran, Doliver, Francis, Joel H., Martin O., Samuel Bent, William Frederick and Mrs. E. A., and not one George — so neither register spelling is a clipped reading of a Walker the town prints otherwise. $4,550.

UPHELD, the same man and the same argument as WALKER G H, and the two are ruled together as cohort A ruled its pairs. This is the spelling the Black Hawk War roll of 1832 prints — 'WALKER, GEORGE H', private in Gholson Kercheval's company — while the Democrat's letter list of 1 April 1834 prints the other, 'G. H. Walker'. Forename in full and middle initial agreeing, on a muster roll that carries a unit and a rank. George E. Walker is refused on the middle initial under rule 2, and his card is `letter_list_only` besides. Lot 1 of block 37 on 22 June 1836, $5,100, on the same page and the same day as G H's lot 6 of the same block: one man, two lots, two spellings. Fergus 1839, Fergus 1843 and Norris 1844 print eleven Walkers between them and no George of any middle initial, so neither reading is clipped from a Walker the town holds under a fuller name.

UPHELD on an office, not a name. The Democrat of 26 November 1833 prints two 'Taken Up' estray notices from Cook County, and the second — a brown horse taken up at Walker's Grove — is appraised by Jeremiah Walker and Timothy J.
